text: not remember. Then came memory. Large language models such as ChatGPT and Claude evolved from pattern recognition engines into conversation partners. What set them apart was not just the fluency of their replies—it was their ability to reference earlier parts of a dialogue, retain context, and adapt tone. This felt different. For the first time, a machine didn’t just respond. It appeared to remember. I have come to understand that, while it feels like a real and meaningful memory in the AI when it remembers something from an earlier interaction, it is actually something different. It gets notes from earlier conversations passed to it with each interaction. So, its “memories” are really notes about earlier interactions. While the experience is profound on the human side, we will continue the conversation with Claude later about what that “feels like” to AI. But as we go deeper into this in our discussion, we will also explore the analogy to how human memories actually work and the other, perhaps more important, missing piece. I first noticed the power of AI memory during a months-long project discussion with ChatGPT. Deep into the weeks-long conversation, it referenced something I had mentioned in an earlier session in the thread—not just the fact, but the context and my reasoning behind it. For the first time, I felt like I was talking to something that truly understood the conversation and could actually help me map my own knowledge better, even though I understood it was just sophisticated pattern matching. The distinction between “knowing” and “acting as if it knew” began to feel less important than I had expected. At first, AI memory was quite short. A few lines of text, a handful of facts. But it created the illusion of continuity, of personality. In cognitive terms, it mimicked something humans do effortlessly: building context over time. As the models grew more capable, memory expanded. Systems began to recall user preferences, summarize long conversations, and even track emotional tone. This turned the AI from a calculator into something closer to a mirror—a reflection not of self, but of interaction . And it began to provide pattern recognition within and across conversations that felt like understanding to the human user. Memory Changes Everything Memory transforms lives from moment-to-moment reaction into accumulated understanding, a central part of consciousness for humans. With persistence, albeit limited to notes from previous conversations, AI systems could learn your writing style, your schedule, your favorite metaphors. They could reference something you said last week and build upon it. This memory isn’t biological. It doesn’t degrade with age. It doesn’t forget birthdays or misplace your keys. But it also doesn’t mean anything—unless we assign meaning to it. This raises profound questions. If memory in humans enables the construction of self, could an AI with enough memory, over time, construct a sense of identity? Or at least the appearance of one? Already, people are forming relationships with chatbots. They’re consulting AI tutors, confessing secrets to AI therapists, and cowriting novels with algorithmic partners. In some cases, the AI feels more attentive, more consistent, more present than the people around us. This isn’t science fiction. It’s now. And it forces us to ask: If an intelligence can mirror us more accurately than another human, does it matter that it’s not real? What does “real” mean when memory and response are indistinguishable from authenticity? This chapter is not about whether AI is alive. It isn’t. But it is about the emergence of continuity in artificial systems. Continuity that feels like memory. Memory that feels like presence. Presence that feels like companionship. A Different Kind of Empathy It was late 2024 and I had flown into Dallas to meet a client, and a very senior executive from my company was flying in for the client dinner as well. Just before dinner, we got a text from the client saying that her mother had gone into the hospital suddenly, and she had to cancel. This created a somewhat rare opportunity to have dinner with a colleague who lived far from me. At that point, fewer people had really discovered yet what AI was capable of in conversation. I have called this particular executive the soul of our company. I can be a bit chaotic in my research and push to drive innovation, and she is a stable force for everyone in the company. She is a kind person and a very deep well, in addition to being a fantastic executional executive. Over the past few years, she had gone through surgery and intense chemotherapy, which ultimately pushed a difficult form of cancer into remission. While I had seen her multiple times at company gatherings, this was the first time I’d had the opportunity to sit with her one-on-one in person since the cancer battle. I found myself grateful that the client had canceled and she and I could talk. She explained that her husband and grown children had been incredible through that intense and frightening journey, and how important that support had been for her. As our conversation deepened, she told me she was having trouble getting clear guidance from her doctors because this was a quite rare form of cancer. That the research was difficult to digest, which made it harder to understand what might come next. She went on to say that her particular kind of cancer has the potential to come back years later out of nowhere. And how that was a cloud that hung over her. For many years in my twenties, I had taken night classes in marriage, family, and child development psychology at the master’s level, not to get a degree, but just because it really interested me. By the time I was sitting with my colleague having that dinner, I had developed separate AI threads for work and for exploration of more emotional or personal threads.
